abstract: Membrane remodeling after pore opening occurs in electroporation, vesicle rupture, intracellular delivery, and pathogen escape from host cells. During this process, a pore may expand or close while the surrounding membrane curls at the rim, forms a neck, or everts. Using a sharp-interface framework for open membranes in Stokes flow, we study how free-edge elasticity and the dissipation mechanism determine post-opening remodeling. The model combines Helfrich bending, Gaussian-curvature and line energies, and local area inextensibility with viscous dissipation in the membrane and the surrounding fluid. We compare it with a local-drag model driven by the same energy over a range of line tensions, Gaussian rigidities, and spontaneous curvatures. Starting from a spherical cap, the membrane first adjusts near the rim as it relaxes toward the free-edge moment condition. The subsequent pore dynamics depend strongly on line tension, with trajectories that either continue to expand or reverse and shrink. Gaussian rigidity changes the rim orientation; for positive Gaussian rigidity, a pronounced internal neck develops behind an outward-moving free edge. Increasingly negative spontaneous curvature localizes deformation near the rim and, at sufficiently negative values, causes the first complete rim turn to precede cap inversion. Hydrodynamic and local-drag simulations can dissipate similar amounts of energy while following different shape trajectories, so in the strongly curved regime the pathway depends on the dissipation model as well as on the energy. Together, the edge tangent angle, neck radius, cap depth, and the relative timing of rim rolling and cap inversion provide measurable geometric signatures that distinguish post-opening remodeling pathways beyond the pore radius.
